newsitem.title: USA: Little rain forecast for N. Dakota, snow melt seen.
newsitem.headline: Little rain forecast for N. Dakota, snow melt seen.

text.p: States such as North Dakota and Montana could see around half their snow melt during the next week but little additional rainfall is forecast, meteorologists said Wednesday.
"By Wednesday of next week they are going to lose between five and 10 inches of snow in those areas," said Fred Gesser, chief forecaster for Weather Express Inc.
He noted on Tuesday the amount of snow in Grand Forks, N.D. had fallen to 15 inches from 17 inches and a further decline was expected over the next few days.
The threat of flooding, however, should not be compounded by significant rainfall, with only light showers forecast.

"They have got flooding already and the snow has got to melt but it could be worse if there were additional rains and right now all we've got is light precipitation-makers coming across which don't offer any big rain," Gesser said.
Light rain was seen falling Thursday, Saturday and Monday.
Joel Burgio, agricultural meteorologist with Weather Services Corp, said the first band of showers, set to move across the area Thursday, should bring about 0.10 to 0.30 inches of rain.
Days of rain were likely to preceded by warm days and followed by cool days, Gesser of Weather Express said.

"Spring is noted for its rapid temperature swings and we do have a active pattern so we are having more swings in temperature than normal for the late March period," Burgio of Weather Services Corp said.
In western and central Kansas, in contrast, the main problem for the hard red winter wheat crop areas have been a lack of moisture, meteorologists said.
WSC's Burgio said that situation appeared unlikely to change during the next few days.
"During the next seven-day period, western Kansas looks set for just a few sprinkles or very light showers," he said.
Gesser of Weather Express said the next significant rains in the region could fall on April 3 or 4 although that was highly speculative.

"It is eight or nine days out (in the computer forecast) and frequently models will offer this thing one day, then it will disappear without a trace the next. It is not time to blow the horn that they are going to get rain," he said.
